title: Pauri 3, meaning: the carefree one
hook: some sing His power, some His gifts; the Giver keeps giving though receivers tire, and He blossoms free of care (Japji 3)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of pauri three: gaavai ko taan, someone sings of strength. Your line was gaavai ko. Did you catch someone singing or humming? Day one hundred sixty-eight.

A grandmother at a family dinner keeps putting food on your plate. You say you're full. She adds another roti. You say really, I'm done. She's already bringing dessert. Eventually you are the one who gives up; she never does. And she seems happy the whole time, not anxious, not keeping count. Guru Nanak's third pauri ends with a picture a little like that, only vast: a Giver who never tires, and receivers who do.
screen: `ANOTHER ROTI ON YOUR PLATE.` → `YOU GIVE UP FIRST.` → `A GIVER WHO NEVER TIRES.`

segments.voice: Here is the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. Some sing of His power, if they have the power. Some sing of His gifts, and know them as His sign. Some sing of His virtues, His greatness and His deeds. Some sing of knowledge gained through hard study. Some sing that He shapes the body and then turns it back to dust. Some that He takes life away and gives it again. Some that He seems far away; some that He watches, face to face, always present. There's no end to the telling; millions upon millions tell it, and still the telling doesn't run out. Then the turn. Dedaa de, laide thak paahi: the Giver keeps giving; the receivers grow tired of receiving. Through age after age, they go on eating. By His order, the One who orders sets the path. And the last line: Nanak, He blossoms, free of care. The word is veparvaahu. Parvaah is worry, concern. Ve means without. Without worry. Carefree. It isn't careless, as in not caring. It's the opposite of anxious. The Giver doesn't give out of need, or to be thanked, or while keeping count. In the pauri's picture, giving is simply what the Giver is. And vigsai, blossoms, is a flower word: opening, delighted. Notice what the pauri does with all those singers from yesterday. It doesn't pick a winner. Power, gifts, far, near: all of them are singing about the same Giver, and none of them finishes. Some readers find relief in that: no singer has to get the song exactly right, and in the pauri the gifts keep coming anyway.
screen: `SOME SING POWER, SOME SING GIFTS.` · `NO END TO THE TELLING.` · `THE GIVER GIVES, RECEIVERS TIRE.` · `VEPARVAAHU — FREE OF CARE.` · then, large: `THE GIVER NEVER TIRES.`

segments.voice: Let's count gifts from today, just three. Start small. The first sip of something warm. A text from someone. The fact that you're breathing without trying. Name the first one quietly. Then the second. Then the third. Don't hurry, and don't pick impressive ones; ordinary is better. Then notice: you didn't make most of them. They arrived. If you pray, you can thank the Giver in a word, Waheguru. If you don't, just let yourself feel given to. The bell holds the time.
Veparvaahu. Free of care: the Giver keeps giving though some sing His power, some His gifts, and there's no end to the telling.
Your line: the giver never tires. Today, give one thing without keeping count. And look back at this week: sach, sochai soch, hukam, hukmee, haumai and gaavai ko. Day one hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite the third pauri each morning in Japji; its closing picture of the carefree Giver is often quoted in talks on gratitude and on giving without counting.

match.prompt: what's inside the pauri — tap the pairs.

myth: it means free of worry: the opposite of anxious, not the opposite of caring.
the pauri says receivers tire before the Giver does
the pauri picks one right way to sing
power, gifts, far, near: all sing of the same Giver, and none finishes.

fork.setup: the Giver keeps giving, age after age. who gets tired first?
fork.reveal: the receivers grow tired of receiving; the Giver goes on, and blossoms, free of care.

original.note: Gurmukhi: the last line of pauri 3: Nanak, He blossoms, free of care.

trapdoor: what you thought: God doesn't care.
what it means: free of worry: a Giver who gives without need, without counting, and blossoms doing it.
what a scholar hears: parvaah comes from Persian, meaning care or concern; with the prefix it means needing nothing from anyone.

sources.ref: Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion (1909), vol. 1, the Japji, pauri 3

notes: Pauri 3 paraphrased after Macauliffe; not quoted.
Veparvaahu: be- (without) + parvaah (Persian parva, care). Confirm etymology and romanization.
Week-end look-back in the carry lists days 162–167.

Review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'Think of'; the closing theology ('giving is what the Giver is', 'the gifts keep coming anyway') now framed as the pauri's picture and some readers' response, not the narrator's assertion to the listener.
